Abstract: The inertness of elemental selenium is a significant obstacle in the synthesis of
selenium-containing materials at low reaction temperatures. Over the years, several recipes have
been developed to overcome this hurdle, however, most of these developed methods are associated
with the use of highly toxic, expensive, and environmentally harmful reagents. As such, there is
an increasing demand for the design of cheap, stable, and non-toxic reactive selenium precursors
usable in the low-temperature synthesis of transition metal selenides with vast applications in
nanotechnology, thermoelectrics, and superconductors. Herein, a novel synthetic route has been
developed for activating elemental selenium using a solvothermal approach. By comprehensive
77Se NMR, Raman, and infrared spectroscopies, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we
show that the activated Se solution contained HSe–, [Se-Se]2–, and Se2– ions, as well as dialkyl
selenide (R2Se) and dialkyl diselenide (R-Se-Se-R) species in dynamic equilibrium. This also
corresponded with the first observation of naked [Se-Se]2– in solution. The versatility of the
developed Se precursor was demonstrated by the successful synthesis of (i) the polycrystalline
room-temperature modification of the β-Ag2Se thermoelectric material; (ii) large single crystals of
superconducting β-FeSe; (iii) CdSe nanocrystals with different particle sizes (3-10 nm); (iv)
nanosheets of PtSe2; and (v) mono- and dibenzyl selenides and diselenides at room temperature.
The simplicity and diversity of the developed Se activation method holds promise for applied and
fundamental research.

children.text:
1. Introduction
Selenium has been a point of focus in materials research over the past few decades, owing to its
high photoconductivity and use for the synthesis of a wealth of chemicals.1–4 Particularly
interesting are metal selenides, which find applications in thermoelectrics, semiconductor quantum
dots, photovoltaics, magnetic semiconductors, and superconductors.5–12 The ubiquitous
applications of selenide materials prompt the need to develop facile, simple, and non-toxic means
of synthesis. The conventional syntheses of transition metal selenides usually involve solid-state
reactions of elements and precursors, chemical vapor deposition, and gas phase reactions.13,14
These reactions require high temperatures, which are energy intensive and may restrict the control
of products. As a result, recent research has focused on low-temperature synthetic routes that
employ soluble selenium precursors.2 One method of solubilizing elemental Se relied upon the use
of KBH4 in ethylenediamine to reduce Se at room temperature and produce nanocrystalline
selenides of different morphologies.15 Although this method involves relatively mild conditions
and less complicated equipment and precursors, as compared to previous works,16,17 the reaction
may produce hazardous byproducts, such as H2Se. When Lu et al. investigated the characteristics
of Se in various solvents, they observed the formation of Se single crystals which was attributed
to a dissolution-recrystallization process.18,19 In chelating solvents, such as ethylenediamine and
ethylenediamine-thiol mixture, Se recrystallization was not observed; instead polynuclear Se
complexes formed.
Trialkylphosphine selenides have also been used as precursors to synthesize high-quality transition
metal selenide nanocrystals.20–23 It has been demonstrated that the phosphine route may be suitable
for materials where surface passivation is required to minimize surface recombination sites;24–26
however, for materials with applications in photovoltaics and sensors, the presence of bulky
surface-bound organic species may impede device performance.27,28 Furthermore, the reaction of
Se with alkyl phosphines such as trioctylphosphine (TOP) and tributylphosphine (TBP) results in
unstable and hazardous products, which are difficult to control even under inert atmospheres.29–
34 This led to the adoption of phosphine-free precursors, which are formed by dissolving Se in
high-boiling-point solvents such as oleylamine, octadecene, olive oil, and paraffin.6–19 It has been
demonstrated that these phosphine-free selenium precursors are more reactive toward particle
growth when compared to their phosphine counterparts.35,36 Unfortunately, this strategy is usually

associated with the formation of H2Se, which acts as a major deactivation pathway during
precursor formation and also poses health concerns.36 Another strategy involves the use of
selenourea and elemental Se under a reductive atmosphere (NaBH4, hydrazine, concentrated
NaOH/KOH), alkyl thiol reduction, and reaction of SeO2 in coordinative solvents.1,32,37–40 Most of
the aforementioned reducing agents are unstable in air and their mechanisms of action are
complicated.29 While these methods produce Se precursors for the synthesis of various metal
selenides, novel, cheap, and environmentally friendly approaches are still actively sought.
A common theme of the proposed synthetic methods is a lack of detailed spectroscopic
characterization of the precursor solutions. Liu et al. reported a room temperature activation of
elemental selenium using octadecene and oleylamine but were unable to fully characterize the
selenium species generated29 beyond the reaction of the generated selenium precursors with metal
ions to confirm the presence of Se2– and a few related species. 77Se NMR and other spectroscopic
studies of the Se solution have been rarely employed.18,32,38,39,41 77Se is a relatively friendly NMR-
active nuclide with a spin of ½, a natural abundance of 7.63 %, and a Larmor frequency of 76.3
MHz at 9.4 T.42 Despite this, there have been only a handful of scientific articles detailing the
study of polyselenides in solution.43–45 Cusick and Dance observed the existence of a fast equilibria
between HSe– and Se2– but could not provide direct NMR evidence for the presence of Se2– in any
of their solutions.44 Similarly, in 2017 Oliveira et al. reported the synthesis and 77Se NMR
characterization of alkyl and aryl selenides and diselenides, but were unable to identify either Se2–
or Se22– ions.43,46 Proper identification of the Se species present in precursor solutions is important
to the rational synthesis of metal selenides.
Herein, we report on a novel synthetic route to activate elemental selenium through a simple
solvothermal treatment by dissolving Se powder in monoethanolamine (2-aminoethan-1-ol). By
varying reaction conditions, different species of selenium were identified and characterized using
77Se NMR, Raman, and FTIR spectroscopies. We demonstrate the existence of Se2– in solution
which was previously believed to be in fast equilibrium with HSe–. In addition, we observe the
presence of Se22– ions in solution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental NMR
report of HSe–, Se22–, and Se2– coexisting in solution. The solution was further assessed to
characterize some organic species associated with the formation of these Se species. A redox
reaction between Se and solvent monoethanolamine molecules was confirmed. We demonstrate

different applications of the activated selenium solution in materials synthesis, ranging from the
low temperature synthesis of thermoelectric β-Ag2Se to the first report of air-stable single crystals
of the β-FeSe superconductor. We also assess the efficacy of the as-synthesized selenium solution
as a suitable reagent for PtSe2 nanosheet and CdSe nanocrystal growth, as well as demonstrate a
way to produce organo-Se species which are suitable for isotopic labeling starting from
isotopically-enriched elemental 77Se.

99.5%), ferrous chloride tetrahydrate (Alfa Aesar, 98%), cadmium iodide (Allied Chemicals &

monoethanolamine (2-aminoethan-1-ol; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 99+%), trioctylphosphine

a glovebox with an argon atmosphere. Monoethanolamine was vacuum degassed in a two-neck
round bottom flask by purging with argon while heating at 100oC for 1 h, cooled to room
temperature, and transferred into an argon-filled glovebox.
2.3 Selenium activation. For typical preparation of the activated Se solution under aerobic
conditions, 1-2 mmol of Se was added in a 23 mL Teflon liner filled with 10 mL of
monoethanolamine (filling fraction 43%), which was tightly closed in a stainless-steel autoclave,

heating process, the autoclave was taken out of the furnace and naturally cooled to room

filter paper produced no residual solid. A similar procedure was carried out in an argon-filled

2.4 Synthesis of β-FeSe. Fe powder (0.4 mmol), NH4Cl (1.87 mmol), and FeCl2·4H2O (0.3 mmol)
were added to the Se solution obtained as described above (1.2 mmol Se), and the reaction vessel
was tightly sealed and heated from 100-210 °C for 3 days. Following natural cooling to room
temperature, the product was filtered and washed with 200-proof ethanol to obtain a mixture of
dark gray to black powder and black plates. The black plates were large enough for conventional
single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. All processes were performed under ambient conditions.
A similar procedure was performed under air-free conditions to obtain polycrystalline samples for
magnetic measurements.
2.5 Synthesis of β-Ag2Se. To a Se solution, prepared as described above using 1 mmol Se and 10
mL monoethanolamine, 2 mmol of AgCl were added at room temperature with continuous stirring
for 30 mins. A dark-gray precipitate was obtained, filtered, and washed with 200-proof ethanol to
reveal a fine dark-gray powder.
2.6 Synthesis of CdSe. The activated Se solution (1.2mmol) was added to a three-neck round-
bottom flask equipped with a reflux condenser and thermocouple. The mixtures were kept at
specified temperatures with constant magnetic stirring. A solution of CdI2 (obtained by dissolving
1.2 mmol CdI2 in 5mL water) was injected and allowed to dwell for a specified duration. Reactions
were carried out at either room temperature or an elevated temperature of 100 °C. In the latter case,
the flask and solution were allowed to cool to room temperature, at which point the mixtures were
centrifuged, decanted, re-dispersed in methanol/hexanes, and sonicated. This process was repeated
until the supernatants became clear, then the nanoparticles were dispersed in methanol/hexanes for
characterization. Details regarding the quantities of materials used and reaction conditions for the
different CdSe nanocrystal (NCs) are given in Table S1.

3. Results and Discussion
3.1 Solvothermal activation of Se. Several methods have been reported for dissolving selenium.
While some of these methods involve room temperature dissolution of selenium powder in highly
reducing solvents such as hydrazine and NaBH4 solutions, other methods employ the solvothermal
treatment of Se powder in high-boiling solvents.29,36,40 The main objective of this study was to
utilize a low-cost and environmentally-friendly solvent to activate elemental selenium and produce
selenide materials with improved properties. As such, we began our investigation by reviewing
previously reported solvents employed for dissolving selenium. Selenium has limited solubility in
ethanol, benzene, and pyridine. Treatment of elemental Se in such solvents often results in
recrystallization and the formation of selenium single crystals. Chelating primary amines and thiols
on the other hand dissolve Se completely with the potential to form polynuclear Se complexes.
With this in mind, we selected monoethanolamine (OH-CH2-CH2-NH2) as a solvent for the
activation process because (i) it is a bifunctional molecule acting as both a primary amine and an
alcohol, and (ii) it is an inexpensive and environmentally-friendly solvent.

specific reaction conditions.

The bifunctional property of monoethanolamine makes it suitable for the complete dissolution of
Se and the subsequent stabilization of reaction products in solution. The process is reversible, as
storage of the solution in air precipitates elemental Se which can be redispersed by a solvothermal
treatment. The versatility of the produced Se solution was demonstrated by the successful synthesis
of various metal selenides with particle sizes varying from a few nanometers to 250 micrometers.
To understand the reaction mechanism and determine the Se species present in the solution,
extensive spectroscopic characterization was performed with findings summarized in Figure 1.
3.2 Characterization of selenium species. We explored the structural chemistry of different Se
species present in solution using 1D and 2D 77Se NMR, Raman, and infrared spectroscopies. 77Se
NMR samples were prepared in neat ethanolamine with the concentration of the solution
maintained at 0.12 M. 77Se NMR spectra were acquired using a gated decoupling sequence with a
30° excitation pulse. The wide 77Se chemical shift range47 (-850 to 1050 ppm) was scanned at room
temperature to identify different Se species present in solution. Chemical shifts were referenced
using the 1H chemical shifts of the solvent and the universal chemical shift referencing scale. 48
In a solution prepared under anaerobic conditions, we observed two 77Se resonances at -667 and -
461 ppm (Figures 2a). The singlet resonating at -667 ppm was assigned to Se2–, which is consistent
with reports by Lyons and Young who measured a singlet resonance at -670 ppm for a 3M solution
of K2Se in 0.1M KOH.46 Odom et al. observed a more deshielded resonance at -511 ppm which
was assigned to Se2–.49 Later studies suggested that there exists a rapid equilibrium between the
Se2– ion and its conjugate acid, HSe–, resulting in resonance line broadening (up to 60 Hz) and
shifting.44 The -667 ppm resonance observed in the present study is sharp (ѵ1/2 = 4.6 Hz),
suggesting an absence of Se2–/HSe– exchange. The observed resonance is further corroborated by
an earlier report from Dance and Cusick who predicted the chemical shift of Se2– to be <-650 ppm
based on their extrapolation from different selenides.44

prepared under ambient reaction conditions. (c) Raman spectrum of the ambient atmosphere Se

A number of previous attempts to detect Se22– in solution have been made. For instance,
McFarlane et al, Eggert et al, Dance et al, and Oliveira et al used 77Se NMR spectroscopy to
investigate the formation and stability of Sex2– (x anions, 43,44,47,50 however, none of these
studies could identify Se 2– species. This observation has been largely attributed to the rapid

disproportionation of the species and coexistence in equilibrium with HSe–, making Se22– difficult
to detect.44 As a result, all resonances observed between -500 to -300 ppm have, to the best of our
knowledge, been assigned to HSe–. This is supported by the resonance’s solvent dependence, with

77Se nuclei being more shielded in protic solvents.44,51 For instance, the 77Se chemical shift of
HSe– are -447 ppm, -495 ppm, and -529 ppm in DMF, ethanol, and water respectively.44,49,52 Given
that monoethanolamine has a polarity that lies between that of DMF and ethanol, we would expect
HSe– to resonate between -447 ppm and -495 ppm in our solutions and display evidence of 77Se-
1H J coupling, either in the form of a splitting, or line broadening.44 Both of these conditions are
met by the broad (ѵ1/2 = 21 Hz) resonance observed at -461 ppm (Figure 2a), which was thus
assigned to HSe–. The chemical shift of Se22– has been estimated to be around -400 ppm using the
125Te chemical shift of Te22– (-1080 ppm).53
To verify whether the presence of oxygen plays a part in the products of the Se solution, powdered
selenium was added to dry monoethanolamine in a glovebox and the mixture was then exposed to
air for a minute before solvothermal treatment. All of the solvothermal liner headspace was filled
with air in this case. 77Se, 1H-coupled, NMR of the solution showed only one signal at -666 ppm
which was assigned to Se2– (Figure S2e). Air exposure of the solution for several days resulted in
Se2– and solid elemental selenium, Se0(s) (Figure S2f). As such, we believe Se2– is robust under
various reaction atmospheres while the other Se species are not, and the formation of HSe– under
the current reaction conditions is influenced by the presence of oxygen.
In a third experiment, a solution was prepared using wet solvent in an ambient atmosphere. 77Se
NMR spectra of this solution (Figures 2b) again featured a sharp resonance at -667 ppm from Se2–
but also contained a second major species at -316 ppm. In accordance with reference [52], we
assigned this species to Se22–. This assignment is further supported by the resonance’s narrow
linewidth (ѵ1/2 = 6 Hz) in a 1H-coupled experiment. Importantly, the lack of 1H–77Se coupling
confirmed that the selenium species is not an organic adduct with Se-C-H bonds. Raman spectra
of the Se22–-containing solution were obtained which indicated the presence of Se–Se stretching
vibrations (Figure 2c).54–56 Two distinct vibrational modes were detected due to the presence of
two diselenide species, Se22– and R-Se-Se-R, discussed below. Although never unambiguously
observed in solution, Se22– is believed to be unstable and disproportionate into Se2– and Se0(s). By
exposing the as-synthesized solution to an ambient atmosphere for several days, we observed the
precipitation of Se0(s) using powder X-ray diffraction (Figure S1). 77Se NMR spectra of the
resulting solution contained a single resonance at -667 ppm from Se2–, providing experimental
evidence for the presence and disproportionation of Se22– in solution.

R–Se–Se–R species in solution prepared under ambient reaction conditions; where R = alkylamino
group. (b) 2D 77Se{1H} INEPT spectra of R–Se–Se–R and R–Se–R species. (c) 77Se solution NMR
spectrum of selenols (RSeH) and selenolates (RSe–) identified in solution prepared under ambient

A number of additional species (δSe = 223, 155, 89, -3, -12 ppm) were also detected in this third
solution, as shown in Figure 3. The resonances at 155 ppm and 223 ppm are the most intense and
display well-resolved J coupling patterns (Figure 3a). Amosova et al have previously observed
that H3C-CH2-Se-CH2-CH2-NH2 has a 77Se chemical shift of 155.9 ppm,57 while (R=N-(CH2)2)2Se
species resonate from 145-151 ppm.58 As such the resonance at 155 ppm can be assigned to a
Se(CH2-CH2-NH2)2 species. The chemical shift for H2N-CH2-CH2-Se-Se-CH2-CH2-NH2 has been
reported to be 234 ppm and that of HO-CH2-CH2-Se-Se-CH2-CH2-OH at 238 ppm.59 Due to the
presence of solvent effects, we cannot conclusively assign the resonance at 223 ppm to either
species, using chemical shifts alone. To obtain further information on the structure of the alkyl
moieties, we performed a 77Se{1H} Insensitive Nuclei Enhancement by Polarization Transfer
experiment (INEPT)-based heteronuclear correlation (HETCOR) experiment (Figure 3b). Both
signals are correlated to 1H sites with chemical shifts of 1.6 and 2.7 ppm, which again agrees with
the values measured by Amosova et al on H3C-CH2-Se-CH2-CH2-NH2 and, as such, both species
are likely aminoethyl mono and diselenides. The presence of a C-Se-C Raman bending mode
(Figure 2c) and a C-Se IR stretch (Figure 2d) provides further support to these assignments.60

The formation of these species under the current reaction conditions is highly promising, as
diorganyl selenides and diselenides are essential Se precursors for the synthesis of colloidal
semiconductor nanocrystals and polymorph-tunable transition metal diselenides.61–63
Of the three remaining minor species, the resonance at 89 ppm most likely originates from HO-
CH2-CH2-Se-CH2-CH2-OH, which has a reported 77Se chemical shift of 85 ppm.64 Due to the low
sensitivity and resolution, it was not possible to discern a multiplet structure for this resonance,
but its linewidth of 33 Hz provided evidence for the presence of 77Se-1H J coupling. We were
unable to conclusively assign the minor resonances at -12 and -3 ppm, but they are most likely
some form of alkyl selenol.
Upon exposure to air for several days, the solution precipitated elemental selenium and 77Se NMR
revealed only the existence of a single sharp resonance at -667 ppm, assigned to Se2– (Figure S1).
This result indicates that Se2– species are stable in solution while the other selenide moieties
disproportionate or are oxidized. Selenols are known to oxidize to diselenides in the presence of
atmospheric oxygen while diselenides disproportionate into Se2– and Se(s).63,65,66 The solution
maintained a dark brown color after the disappearance of these unstable species, but the color
faded away after air-exposure for several months. Thus the monoselenide species, Se2–, can be
stabilized in solution for several months before being oxidized to Se0.
Dialkyl/diaryl selenides and diselenides are recognized as versatile molecular precursors for
isolating metastable poly- and nanocrystalline phases with interesting properties.61,67,68 The
reactivity of these precursors is linked to the bond dissociation energies of the Se-Se and C-Se
bonds, and these precursors allow for control over the phase and morphology of reported
nanocrystals.62,68,69 The current Se activation strategy enables the in situ generation of
dialkyl/diaryl diselenide species at room temperature. The addition of benzylchloride to a freshly
prepared Se solution produced dibenzyldiselenide and dibenzylselenide (Figure S6), which are
known to be valuable precursors for the synthesis of selenide nanocrystals, in addition to novel
organoselenide species.43,68 The latter can be useful for isotopic labeling with 77Se, as the starting
material is elemental Se which is the most common commercial source of 77Se.70,71

the Se dissolution kinetics. A mixture of Se powder and monoethanolamine was solvothermally
treated at different temperatures (140–210 °C) for varying reaction times. The dissolution time
was taken to be the point at which no residual solid Se was observed in solution after filtration. An
exponential activation rate was observed for the dissolution process in which there was a sharp
decrease in time with increasing temperature from 140 to 180 °C and a gradual change in
dissolution time above 180 °C. Specifically, it took 15 h to completely dissolve Se at 140 °C, while
at 210 °C the complete dissolution was achieved after 1 h.
Figure 5. (a) Natural log of the amount of selenium recovered (in mg) against reaction time at 160
°C with the slope corresponding to the rate constant (k). (b) The natural log of reciprocal
dissolution time plotted against 1000/T which indicates the temperature dependence of the
dissolution process.
The dissolution process was further investigated at 160 °C to estimate the rate constant as well as
the reaction order. The time-dependence of Se dissolution was determined by directly measuring
the yield of solid Se after reaction. A plot of the natural log of solid selenium obtained as a function
of dissolution time follows a linear path with slight deviation (at t = 0 and 3600s) attributed to the
time needed to warm the stainless-steel autoclaves (Figure 5a). The negative slope graph is
indicative of a first order process with a rate constant of 2.72(3)×10–4 s–1. The reaction order was
further verified from the temperature dependence (Figure 5b). Since the reaction rate is a first

order process, the activation energy can be estimated using the Arrhenius equation. Using this
relation, an activation energy of 67(2) kJ/mol was determined.
Following its thorough characterization, we utilized the produced activated Se solution to produce
various selenides to verify its application in materials synthesis.
3.4 Superconducting β-FeSe single crystals. While several solution routes have been used for
the synthesis of β-FeSe, superconductivity was only observed in a few of these methods.72
Superconductivity was shown to be negatively impacted by the presence of moisture and air during
either the synthesis or post-synthetic sample storage and handling.73 This may be caused by the
general difficulty in growing large crystals of β-FeSe; a majority of solution routes produce
crystals that have a plate-like morphology with thicknesses of only a few tens of nm.48, 49 As of
yet, the dependence of superconductivity on particle size is unknown, in large part due to the
aforementioned challenges with solution synthesis. Unlocking the ability to grow large crystals of
β-FeSe from solution may be the key to restoring its superconductivity under ambient reaction
conditions. Previous reports of single crystal growth of β-FeSe involved high temperature flux or
vapor transport syntheses.76 High temperature synthetic routes towards β-FeSe are usually
accompanied with impurity phases and further limited by the high vapor pressure of selenium –
resulting in the loss of superconductivity and further complicating the study of the material’s
structure-property relationships.9,72,77,78
Large superconducting crystals of β-FeSe were grown in aerobic conditions by solvothermal
reaction of the aforementioned activated Se solution with mixture of elemental Fe and FeCl2⋅4H2O
in the presence of an NH4Cl mineralizer. All handling and syntheses were done under an ambient
atmosphere. The Se solution initiated the oxidation of elemental Fe at temperatures just above 100
°C. Phase-pure polycrystalline β-FeSe samples were produced within a temperature range of 180-
210 °C and a reaction duration of 3-5 days. The crystallinity and phase purity of the as-synthesized
β-FeSe was confirmed with PXRD. The width of the diffraction peaks indicated that the as-
synthesized β-FeSe crystallites are not nanostructured, contrary to reports for other samples

confirm the crystal structure of β-FeSe (Inset of Figure 6a, Table S1). Rietveld analysis of

This composition was consistent with that refined from SCXRD and Rietveld refinement (Table
S1). Similar to superconducting β-FeSe produced by solid-state synthesis, samples from the
present study do not exhibit any magnetic ordering near 50 K. A magnetic anomaly was, however,
observed around 120 K, which is analogous to that observed in other iron chalcogenide systems
(Figure S7).72,80 We attribute this anomaly to a surface layer of Fe3O4. Polycrystalline samples
exhibit a superconducting transition around 9 K (Figure 6b), with ~20% superconducting
shielding volume fraction at a 5 Oe applied AC field for samples synthesized under ambient
conditions. Controlled synthesis under inert conditions, i.e. in an Ar-filled glovebox resulted in
similar samples with close to 20% superconducting volume fraction (Figure S8).

robustness of the superconducting properties of the as-synthesized material under the current
synthetic conditions.
3.5 Thermoelectric β-Ag2Se. Another transition metal selenide explored in the present study is
thermoelectric β-Ag2Se. This room temperature modification of silver selenide has a complex
crystal structure with 3- and 4-coordinated Ag atoms. At ~134 °C, a β→ α transition occurs
yielding cubic α-Ag2Se polymorph with superionic conducting properties and potential Ag
vacancies.40,81 The charge and thermal transport properties of the β-Ag2Se are sensitive to the
synthetic route employed which often requires high temperatures to form α-Ag2Se first, followed
by an α→ β transformation upon cooling. To bypass this constraint, the synthesis and processing
of β-Ag2Se must be performed at temperatures below the β→α phase transition (134 °C).82
Treating AgCl with the activated Se solution at 80 °C, a dark-gray powder was obtained and
characterized by PXRD. Rietveld refinement (Figure 6g) confirmed the formation of the
orthorhombic β-Ag2Se polymorph (JCPDS 24-1041, also known as naumannite). SEM/EDX was
employed to confirm the morphology and stoichiometric ratio of Ag:Se respectively (Figures
6c&d). The characterization of the thermoelectric properties of the as-synthesized β-Ag2Se are

(a few microns) is smaller than that for β-FeSe.
3.6 CdSe nanocrystals. Cadmium selenide (CdSe) nanocrystals have attracted immense research
interest due to their size-tunable optical and electronic properties.83,84 Many successful attempts
have been made to synthesize size-tunable CdSe nanoparticles by employing various cadmium
and selenium precursors.35 Typical syntheses involve the preparation of soluble Se precursors
using bulky organic solvents/ligands followed by hot injection of soluble cadmium salts at higher
temperatures.84 Although lower temperature syntheses of magic-sized CdSe clusters have been
reported, this approach is cumbersome and involves the use of highly air-sensitive selenium
sources which are known to form undesirable byproducts.31 CdSe nanocrystals (NCs) were
synthesized to probe the applicability of the activated Se solution developed herein. A water
solution of CdI2 was injected into the activated selenium precursor at room temperature to produce
CdSe nanoparticles (<10nm). The use of varying synthetic temperature and capping ligands altered
the size of the produced nanoparticles (refer to Supporting Information for the synthetic details).
According to PXRD, the resulting CdSe nanocrystals crystallize in the wurtzite structure type
(Figure S11a). The morphology, phase crystallinity, and elemental composition of these
nanoparticles were confirmed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Figure S12). UV-
Vis absorption spectra of the CdSe NCs (Figure S13) show that the nanocrystals have strong
absorption in the visible region. The respective bandgaps at these absorption edges were
determined by extrapolating the linear region of plots of the squared absorbance versus photon
energy (Figure S10). Using a previously proposed relation, the nanoparticle sizes were determined
from their respective measured optical bandgaps (Figure S11b).85
This new synthetic route for the synthesis of CdSe quantum dots with variable crystallite size is a
case study to demonstrate that the new Se solubilization strategy is a viable synthetic strategy and
a plausible avenue to modulate the size of these nanoparticles. Further synthetic modifications
such as high-temperature injection, using alternate cadmium precursors, and varying the capping
ligands may enable the tuning of nanoparticle size distribution.
3.7 Platinum diselenide nanosheets. PtSe2 is an emergent 2D transition metal dichalcogenide
(TMDC) material with interesting physical and electronic properties, making it suitable for a wide
range of applications ranging from optoelectronics to catalysis.86–88 The synthesis of 2D PtSe2 with

desired thickness, crystallinity, and size for specific applications is challenging.89 The material’s
micro- and nanostructure have been shown to be highly dependent on the method of synthesis.
Several successful approaches have been adopted to synthesize size and thickness-tunable
nanosheets of PtSe2; however, such syntheses have been limited by the complexity and cost of
these methods. We used the as-prepared Se solution to synthesize PtSe2 nanosheets. A simple two-
step approach was adopted: (1) treatment of the Se solution with PtCl2 at room temperature to
obtain a [PtSe] complex, followed by (2) thermal treatment of the [PtSe] complex to form PtSe2
nanosheets.

The crystallinity, phase purity, and nano-layered nature of the as-synthesized PtSe2 was confirmed
by PXRD (Figure 7a), while EDX was employed to determine the elemental composition (Table
S3). All diffraction peaks can be indexed to trigonal PtSe2 with no additional peaks evident within
the instrument limit. The diffraction peaks exhibit different degrees of broadening with 00l peaks
being much broader than hk0 ones, indicating the highly anisotropic nature of crystallites with
Scherrer size estimates ranging between 3 to 10 nm. To verify that the activated Se solution was
crucial for the formation of the PtSe2, we performed a control experiment using thoroughly ground
Se powder and PtCl2, then thermally treated the resultant mixture under the same reaction

indicated a mixture of phases: PtSe2, Pt4Se5, and Pt (Figure S14). This control experiment
highlights the importance of the activated Se solution for the formation of single-phase PtSe2
within the limits of PXRD and EDX.
Raman spectroscopy has been widely used to study TMDCs due to their strong interlayer coupling
and hybridization.89 Most TMDCs including PtSe2, adopt a CdI2-type lattice with point group
symmetry D3d due the thermodynamic stability of the 1T-phases, and exhibit four characteristic
vibrational modes: two Raman active modes (A1g and Eg) and two IR modes (Eu and A2u).89,90
Based on previous experimental and computational reports, the two Raman active modes are
expected to occur around 180 and 210 cm–1 for the in-plane (Eg) and out-of-plane (A1g) vibrations
of Se atoms, respectively.87,89,91 Note that the exact position and intensity of these Raman modes
are dependent on the thickness of PtSe2. A room-temperature Raman spectrum collected on the as-
synthesized PtSe2 nanosheets revealed two Raman modes consistent with the reported modes and
further confirmed the sample purity (Figure 7b). We observed an in-plane mode around 179 cm– 1
and an out-of-plane mode at 208 cm–1 which indicates that the synthesized PtSe2 nanosheets are
only a few layers thick. We also observed that the Eg peak is much more intense than the A1g peak
with an A1g/Eg maximum intensity ratio of 0.3. The stark difference in these peak intensities has
been observed for relatively thin 2D van der Waals crystals and is attributed to the suppression of
van der Waals interlayer interactions.89,92,93 Comparing the relative Raman peak positions and the
A1g/Eg ratio to reported values for PtSe2 and other TMDCs, the produced herein PtSe2 nanosheets
are at least 5 layers thick.

microstructure of the PtSe2 nanosheets. Figures 8a and 8c depict high resolution bright field TEM

4. Discussion
Generalizing the synthetic efforts and knowledge of the activated Se solution produced in this
work, we hypothesize that the multiple observed Se species exist in dynamic equilibrium.
Reactions with metal ions results in a depletion of Se2– from the solution, which is then replenished
by other forms of dissolved Se, such as Se22– and R-Se-Se-R. The crystallite sizes of the produced
metal selenides are controlled by the concentration or dissolution rate of corresponding metal ions.
When CdI2 and PtCl2 are used as sources of Cd and Pt, well-dispersed solutions of Cd2+ and Pt2+
react with Se2– to promptly forming nanocrystals of CdSe and the [PtSe] complex, respectively.
Thermal treatment converts the [PtSe] complex into PtSe2 nanosheets. Slowing of the ion
exchange, as in the case of silver, is achieved by utilizing an insoluble AgCl precursor which has
lower reactivity and thus forms micron-sized β-Ag2Se particles. Finally, for the formation of iron
selenide, elemental Fe is used as a precursor. An oxidation of Fe is required to form β-FeSe
(Fe0→Fe2+) and is accompanied by the reduction of various Se–1 species to Se2–. The slow rate of
this process resulted in the growth of large, submillimeter crystals. We believe that the proposed
method of Se activation will find broad applications in the synthesis of various functional materials
owing to its simplicity, low-temperature nature, and the ability to achieve variable particle size. In
addition, this method provides a potentially efficient means of producing 77Se-enriched organic
species such as Se-containing proteins for NMR analysis.
The developed activated Se solution serves as a universal precursor for synthesizing selenium
containing materials for applications ranging from thermoelectrics and optoelectronics to
superconductors and transition metal dichalcogenide nanosheets. Furthermore, the dissolved Se
species readily reacts with alkyl and dialkyl halides at room temperature to form alkyl and dialkyl
selenides and diselenides that may find use in protein chemistry studies and nanocrystal syntheses.
The reactants and conditions employed in the Se activation process are safe, cheap, and
environmentally-friendly. The dissolution is also reversible given that solutions stored in air
precipitate elemental Se which can then be redissolved via thermal treatment. When compared
with previously reported activation processes, the current Se activation strategy overcomes
challenges associated with highly coordinating and long-chain alkyl amine ligands/solvents, which
can hinder device performance in thermoelectrics and photovoltaics. Finally, the use of this
activated Se solution for the near-room temperature synthesis of functional materials promotes

children.text:
We have demonstrated a simple yet powerful solvothermal route to activate elemental selenium
via reduction and solvation by monoethanolamine. A combination of 77Se NMR, Raman, FTIR,
and GC-MS characterizations revealed that various Se species with –2 and –1 formal oxidation
states are present in the produced solution in dynamic equilibrium. The present study provides the
first experimental NMR evidence of naked Se22– species in solution. The dissolution is reversed
by exposing the sample to air which oxidizes the selenide species in solution and precipitates
elemental Se. We showed that the produced Se solution is a highly viable selenium source for the
synthesis of metal selenide materials with improved properties. Utilizing the developed Se
precursor, we successfully synthesized (i) β-FeSe single crystals with robust superconducting
properties under ambient conditions; (ii) single phase samples of the low-temperature modification
of thermoelectric silver selenide, β-Ag2Se, (iii) CdSe nanocrystals with varying particle sizes and
corresponding optical properties, and (iv) PtSe2 nanosheets with thickness ranging from 3 to 10
nm (5-15 layers). Crystallite sizes appear to be controlled by the solubility of the metal reagent.
Finally, we established a room temperature route to synthesizing aryl selenide and diselenide
precursors – which are vital components in the synthesis of semiconductor nanocrystals. Thus, the
described methodology demonstrates that starting from elemental Se provides a facile route to
produce reduced selenium species that were previously challenging to access via solution
chemistry and are vital for the synthesis Se-containing functional materials.
